Maladaptive Strategies.value: I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible
constantly check body for signs of danger or injury
I detach myself from the memories

Threat.value: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Negative Appraisals.value: I acted in ways that go against who I am
Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

vignette: At twenty, Kwame was ambushed behind a row of industrial warehouses on a rain-slicked street. He remembered the sudden screech of tires, the heavy thud of a sedan door slamming shut beside him, and the overwhelming, crushing weight of multiple bodies pinning his arms. He had fought until his voice gave out, but the rapid escalation and the disorienting spin of the world stripped him of any ability to steer the situation. He lay paralyzed on the wet asphalt while they violated him, the rhythmic bass from the vehicle's speakers syncing with his own ragged breathing, leaving him utterly stripped of autonomy. When they finally shoved him away and peeled out into the night, he remained trembling in the alley, convinced the chaos was entirely his fault and that anyone with a fraction of his strength should have stopped it. In the months that followed, the professional kitchen where Kwame now worked as a line cook became a landscape of unrelenting threat. The clatter of pots, the sharp strike of a knife against a cutting board, and the sudden revving of delivery trucks outside the loading dock instantly dragged the full, unfiltered weight of that night back into his mind. Because his core beliefs fractured around the event, his conviction that he had fundamentally violated his own values and that others should have intervened warped how the memories surfaced. Instead of processing coherently, the recollections arrived as fragmented, sensory shards accompanied by phantom echoes of the men's voices and the sedan's brakes. His hopelessness about his future cemented this pattern, ensuring that ordinary stimuli were instantly filtered through the lens of past violation, which directly heightened his sensitivity to environmental triggers. Now, at twenty-one, Kwame navigates his days in a state of tight coiling. When he hears a car backfire on the street below his apartment, the false alarm ignites instantly, throwing him on guard and scanning the room for sudden movements. His alertness at home bleeds directly into his shifts at the restaurant, where a waiter's abrupt turn or a manager's raised voice triggers an immediate fight-or-flight posture. Every spike of perceived threat automatically pulls the auditory echoes of the assault back into his awareness, which then floods his mind and directly forces him into defensive habits. To cope with the flooding sensations, he has adopted a rigid routine of constantly checking his body for signs of danger or injury, while simultaneously forcing himself to mentally detach from the vivid flashes. Yet the very act of numbing himself only ensures the memories continue to surface unprocessed, and the revenge fantasies he nurses during these detached intervals only harden his sense of moral failure and hopelessness. The cumulative toll has fractured his professional life and personal relationships. He has started leaving his station mid-service whenever a truck idles too long in the alley, citing sudden nausea to the head chef, who has grown wary of his unreliability. Friends have stopped calling, unsure how to reach the young man who now flinches at every sudden gesture and speaks of his days in flat, defeated tones. What finally brought Kwame to seek help was a tremor that would not stop during a prep shift, forcing him to drop a tray of knives and realize he was no longer eating or sleeping, only waiting. He sits now on the clinic chair, most afraid of losing the fragile control he has carved out through his routines, yet quietly hoping to find a way to finally step out of the alley that never seems to end.
